meta.description: Genuinely Churchill — House of Commons, 20 August 1940, recorded in Hansard. Still in copyright until 2035 (Churchill Literary Estate, via Curtis Brown). And his very next sentence pivots from Fighter Command to the bomber crews.

answer.label: Spoken by
answer.authorDates: 1874–1965 · British prime minister and Nobel laureate
answer.sourceLine: House of Commons, 20 August 1940, in the ‘War Situation’ debate during the Battle of Britain — recorded in Hansard at vol 364, cols 1166–67. It is genuinely his, word for word. The detail almost always lost is what follows it: he immediately turns from the fighter pilots to the bomber crews flying ‘night after night, month after month’ into Germany.

source.heading: The source
source.excerpt: The gratitude of every home in our Island, in our Empire, and indeed throughout the world, except in the abodes of the guilty, goes out to the British airmen who, undaunted by odds, unwearied in their constant challenge and mortal danger, are turning the tide of the world war by their prowess and by their devotion. Never in the field of human conflict was so much owed by so many to so few.
trail: Hansard records the speech in the ‘War Situation’ debate of 20 August 1940, with the sentence in its full context of gratitude to the airmen Hansard, HC Deb 20 Aug 1940 ↗.
The International Churchill Society publishes the speech — known as ‘The Few’ — confirming the wording and the setting during the Battle of Britain ‘The Few’ ↗.

Read on in Hansard and the emphasis shifts: ‘All hearts go out to the fighter pilots… but we must never forget that all the time, night after night, month after month, our bomber squadrons travel far into Germany.’ The line is popularly read as being about Fighter Command alone; Churchill deliberately widened it the next sentence ↗.
source.excerptNote: The famous sentence with the one preceding it, which supplies the ‘so many’ and the ‘so few.’ Quoted alone it is a tribute; quoted in place it is the conclusion of an argument.

source.rightsNote: In copyright. Churchill died on 24 January 1965, so his speeches are protected in the UK and EU until the end of 2035; the US term for 1940s works runs to broadly the same period. The literary estate’s permissions are administered by Curtis Brown. Practically: quoting this sentence in a talk, article or book with attribution is normal quotation practice and nobody seeks a licence for it. Reproducing a long passage of the speech, or putting the line on merchandise, is the case that gets licensed and enforced — and using Churchill’s name to sell goods raises estate and brand issues quite apart from copyright. This is not legal advice.

author.name: Winston Churchill
author.heading: About Winston Churchill
author.metaLine: 1874–1965 · British prime minister, statesman & Nobel laureate in Literature
author.bio: Sir Winston Churchill led Britain through the Second World War and won the 1953 Nobel Prize in Literature for his historical writing and oratory. He delivered this on 20 August 1940, in the middle of the Battle of Britain, when the outcome was genuinely undecided. Because so many invented aphorisms are pinned on him, it is worth stating plainly when a famous line is entirely his — this one is, and it is in Hansard.

misattribution.heading: Correctly credited — watch the wording and the context
misattribution.intro: The attribution is solid and the citation is exact. What goes wrong is small drift in the words, and a much larger drift in what people think the sentence is about.

items.why: Hansard has ‘human conflict.’ Both substitutes circulate widely, and an inserted comma (‘by so many, to so few’) is common too Hansard ↗.

It is universally read as a tribute to the fighter pilots — and it is — but Churchill’s very next sentence insists on the bomber squadrons too. Quoting the line alone quietly narrows what he was doing.
Its age misleads: a 1940 speech feels historic enough to be public domain, but Churchill died in 1965 and the estate’s rights run to 2035 permissions ↗.

misattribution.truthLine: Genuinely Churchill, House of Commons, 20 August 1940, recorded in Hansard — and still in copyright until 2035 official record ↗.

context.heading: Why it resonates
lead: The Battle of Britain was still being fought when he said it, and the disproportion he names is literal: a few thousand aircrew standing between an island and invasion. The sentence works because it is arithmetic, not metaphor.
It has since become the template for thanking any small group who carried something enormous — which is a fair inheritance, if one that has drifted a long way from RAF Fighter Command in August 1940.
detailsBody: Before: ‘The gratitude of every home in our Island… goes out to the British airmen who, undaunted by odds… are turning the tide of the world war.’
The line: ‘Never in the field of human conflict was so much owed by so many to so few.’
After: ‘All hearts go out to the fighter pilots… but we must never forget that all the time, night after night, month after month, our bomber squadrons travel far into Germany.’
context.pull: The sentence everyone quotes; the sentence after it is the one everyone forgets.
